opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to matter a lot, but maybe not in the way people usually assume. The obvious part is manufacturing. A robot arm today might cost tens of thousands of dollars. That's not because the motors and gears are inherently that expensive. It's because these things are built in fairly small volumes, often for industrial customers who need extreme precision and reliability. When you go from making thousands of units to making millions, the per-unit cost drops a lot. We've seen that with cars, phones, and drones.

The more interesting part is how the intelligence side interacts with the hardware side. Historically, robots had to be very precise and rigid, because the control software assumed the robot would go exactly where you told it. That precision is expensive: stiff materials, high-quality encoders, carefully machined parts. If you have learned controllers that can use feedback, look at the world through a camera, and correct their mistakes the way a person does, the hardware can get much cheaper. People aren't precise machines either. We're kind of floppy and imprecise, and we make up for it with perception and adaptation. So better learning lets you use worse hardware, which makes it cheaper, which means you can deploy more of it.

That sets up a flywheel. Cheaper robots mean more robots out in the world. More robots collect more data, and more data makes the models better. Better models tolerate cheaper, less precise hardware. I think that loop matters more than any single manufacturing improvement. I'd also guess that once that loop really gets going, the cost of a reasonably capable mobile manipulator could come down to something closer to the cost of a car, or even less. At that point the question stops being whether you can afford a robot and becomes what useful work you can get it to do. That brings you back to the intelligence problem, which I think has always been the real bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response says robot arms may cost tens of thousands of dollars today and discusses manufacturing scale, but it does not identify a roughly tenfold price decline from the arms Levine bought for his Berkeley lab to those used at Physical Intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that capable mobile manipulators could eventually cost about as much as a car or less, but it does not state that Physical Intelligence's current roughly $3,000 arms could be made for a small fraction of that cost.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing to keep in mind is that robots, at least physically, are not that complicated. If you look at the actual components in a modern robot arm, or even a humanoid, it's motors, gearboxes, some sensors, cameras, a battery, some compute. None of that is exotic. It's roughly the same bill of materials as a car, and arguably simpler, because you don't need to withstand the same kinds of forces or operate at highway speeds. So the question is really why robots are expensive today, and the answer is almost entirely volume. When you manufacture something in the hundreds or thousands, you pay for engineering amortization, you pay for custom machining, you pay for low-volume suppliers. When you manufacture in the millions, all of that collapses.

Cars are actually a nice reference point. A car has thousands of precision parts, has to be safe at high speed, and you can buy one for twenty or thirty thousand dollars. There's no fundamental reason a general-purpose robot should cost more than that, and I think there are good reasons it could cost quite a bit less, maybe closer to what a high-end appliance costs. The arms people use in research labs today are tens of thousands of dollars each, but the ones coming out of newer companies are already an order of magnitude cheaper, and that's without anything like automotive-scale production.

But the interesting part to me is that the hardware cost isn't really the bottleneck. The reason there isn't volume is that the robots can't do enough useful things yet. It's a chicken and egg problem. You don't get economies of scale until there's demand, and you don't get demand until the robots are capable, and the capability comes from the learning and the data, which in turn comes from having lots of robots deployed. So I think what actually breaks the cycle is the software side. Once you have a foundation model for robots that's general enough that a robot can be useful out of the box across a wide range of tasks, then the demand materializes, then the volumes go up, and then the hardware gets cheap very quickly. Hardware follows software here, not the other way around.

There's also a second-order effect that I think is underappreciated. When you have really capable learning-based control, you can tolerate much worse hardware. A lot of the cost in traditional robotics comes from precision: very stiff joints, very accurate encoders, very repeatable motion, because the classical control approach assumes you can command a position and the robot will go exactly there. A learned policy that's closing the loop through vision doesn't need that. It can compensate for backlash, for compliance, for a camera that's slightly misaligned. So the better the models get, the cheaper the acceptable hardware becomes, which is another positive feedback loop on cost.

So my expectation is something like a step function rather than a gradual decline. Costs stay fairly high while robots are a niche product, and then once they cross a capability threshold where they're broadly useful, you get a very rapid drop, probably a lot faster than people expect, because the underlying components were never the hard part.

r002.rationale: It suggests general-purpose robots could eventually cost closer to a high-end appliance, but does not state that Physical Intelligence’s roughly $3,000 arms could be made for a small fraction of that price.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of room for the cost to come down. A robot is, at some level, motors, gears, electronics, and a battery. Those things can be expensive when you’re building a few hundred units, but they don’t necessarily have to be expensive when you’re building millions. A car is a pretty complicated robot, mechanically speaking, and we’re quite good at manufacturing those at scale.

The challenge is getting to that scale. If the robot can only do one very narrow task, then the market for that particular machine might be fairly small. You have to recover the engineering costs over a small number of units. If you can build a more general-purpose robot, and use essentially the same hardware for lots of different jobs, then you can spread those costs over a much larger number.

So I think the intelligence and the hardware cost are connected. Better intelligence makes the robot useful in more places, which creates the demand that lets you manufacture it more cheaply. And then the lower price makes still more applications economically viable. The difficult part is getting that process started.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention $3,000 robot arms at Physical Intelligence or say they could be made for a small fraction of that cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardware could get a lot cheaper. If you look at a robot arm today, it’s often a fairly specialized piece of equipment produced in relatively small quantities. The price reflects that. It doesn’t necessarily tell you what it would cost to manufacture millions of them.

But there’s a chicken-and-egg problem. To manufacture millions of robots, you need millions of people who want to buy them. And for people to want to buy them, the robots have to do something useful. So I think a lot hinges on the intelligence: can we make a robot sufficiently capable that there’s a broad market for essentially the same hardware?

That also means the relevant cost isn’t just the purchase price. If you have a cheap robot that needs a person to intervene every few minutes, that’s a very expensive system to operate. A more expensive robot that reliably works all day could be much more economical. So economies of scale will help with the hardware, but reliability and generality are what let you reach that scale in the first place.
